blocks.h: 1. Where the energy to be recovered is

blocks.p: A screw propeller working behind a hull typically converts only about 65 to 72 per cent of delivered power into useful thrust. The losses are of three kinds: axial, in the sternward momentum of the race; rotational, in the swirl the blades impart to it; and frictional and vortex losses, principally the hub vortex shed from the boss. The rotational component alone is commonly of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power on a single-screw merchant ship.

The rudder is the only large body standing in that race. It is therefore both an opportunity - the swirl arrives at it already rotating, so a correctly oriented surface there sees an angle of attack for nothing - and a liability, because a plain rudder behind a bare boss adds drag and lets the hub vortex run on unchecked. The four devices below exploit the first and reduce the second.

A rudder thrust fin is a horizontal foil, usually fitted as a pair port and starboard, mounted on the rudder at or near the level of the propeller shaft, inside the slipstream. Because the race is rotating, the flow arrives at the fin with a tangential component: upward on one side of the shaft and downward on the other. Each fin is set at the angle that turns that oncoming flow into lift, and because the flow is inclined, the lift vector is tilted forward. Its horizontal component is thrust, generated with no additional power.

ul: The two fins are set at different angles, or in mirror image, because the swirl direction differs above and below the shaft.
Gains quoted in industry literature are typically of the order of 2 to 5 per cent in delivered power, and are strongly dependent on span, chord and angle of attack.
The angle is fixed at build. The device is optimised for one draught and speed and gives less, or in extreme off-design conditions nothing, elsewhere.
It is a source of added appendage drag when not loaded, and a candidate for cavitation erosion if it sits too close to the blade tips.

blocks.p: Here the recovery is built into the rudder itself rather than added to it. On a single-screw ship the propeller turns one way, so the race strikes the upper half of the rudder from one side and the lower half from the other. A conventional symmetrical rudder, aligned with the centreline, therefore meets the flow at an angle of attack of the wrong sign over half its span, producing side force, drag and early cavitation.

An asymmetric rudder cures this by making the two halves different. In the developed form - the twisted leading edge rudder - the leading edge is twisted in opposite directions above and below the shaft line, so that each half is aligned with the swirl it actually meets.

ul: The rudder becomes a swirl-recovery surface: the side force on the two halves is turned into a net forward component.
It reduces drag and cavitation, and with it rudder erosion and propeller-excited vibration.
It is handed - built for one direction of rotation - so it is a design decision, not a universal retrofit.
Because it changes the rudder body rather than adding to it, it carries no added appendage and its benefit degrades more gracefully off design than a fixed fin.

blocks.p: The propeller boss sheds a strong hub vortex, and behind a bare boss the flow separates, leaving a low-pressure wake that pulls the ship astern. A rudder bulb is a streamlined body of revolution fitted to the rudder leading edge, coaxial with the shaft and sized and positioned so that it forms an almost continuous body with the propeller hub cap, closing the gap between them.

ul: It suppresses or displaces the hub vortex, removing a pure loss.
It restores pressure behind the boss by giving the flow a body to close around instead of separating, which is a genuine reduction in resistance rather than a recovery of energy.
The diameter and the axial gap govern the result; too large or too far aft and the bulb adds more drag than it saves.
It is most often fitted together with fins, the bulb conditioning the flow the fins work in, so the two are designed as one installation and their savings are not simply additive.

blocks.p: The vane wheel, patented by Otto Grim in 1966, is the most ambitious of the four and the only one that moves. It is a freely rotating bladed wheel mounted on the shaft line immediately aft of the propeller, of larger diameter than the propeller, with no mechanical connection to it or to the shaft. It runs at its own speed, typically around a third to a half of propeller revolutions, driven entirely by the water.
Its cleverness is that one blade does two jobs at different radii:

ol: The inner portion, standing inside the propeller race, works as a turbine. It extracts energy from the swirl and axial velocity of the slipstream, and that is what drives the wheel round.

The outer portion, standing outside the race in undisturbed water, works as a propeller. Driven by the torque the inner part has extracted, it produces additional thrust over a larger disc area and therefore at higher efficiency.

blocks.p: The wheel thus takes wasted energy from a small, fast, disturbed stream and returns it as thrust in a large, slow, clean one. Gains of the order of 5 to 10 per cent were claimed and some were demonstrated. In service the device proved difficult: the long, thin, unsupported blades of the outer portion are fatigue-loaded and blade loss and shedding occurred; performance falls away in a seaway and off design, when the wheel can windmill unhelpfully; and it adds a rotating component aft of the propeller with its own bearing and clearance problems. It is now of more importance as a principle - and as an examination question - than as a device in general service.

blocks.h: 6. Whether a claimed gain is real on this ship

blocks.p: All four claims are hull-specific. A device recovers only what the propeller behind that hull actually wastes, so the gain depends on the wake field, block coefficient, propeller loading, draught and service speed. Three consequences follow, and they are where the marks are at this level. First, a quoted percentage means nothing without the condition it was measured in, and model-scale results require a scale-effect correction before they can be believed at full scale. Second, devices interact: a bulb changes the flow the fins see, so savings must be assessed for the installation as a whole. Third, the real case is the operating profile - a ship that spends its life slow-steaming at part draught will not realise a gain optimised for design condition, and the payback calculation must be built on the actual profile, on class approval of the attachment and its structure, and on the effect on manoeuvring, which a rudder-mounted device necessarily touches.

The examiner has done the structuring for you. Four devices are named and each carries 4 marks, so the answer is four equal blocks and nothing else can be substituted for them. The single most common way to lose marks here is to write a good general essay on energy-saving devices - pre-swirl stators, ducts, propeller boss cap fins, air lubrication - none of which is asked for. Answer the four printed limbs.

blocks.h: The one idea that unlocks all four

blocks.p: Rotational loss. The propeller leaves the race spinning, and that spin is energy already paid for and thrown away. Two of these devices recover it - the fin and the twisted rudder turn swirl into forward force, and the vane wheel takes it mechanically. Two stop further waste - the bulb removes the hub vortex and the separation behind the boss. If you can say which of the two categories a device is in, you can reconstruct its explanation from first principles.

blocks.h: Keep recovery and drag reduction apart

ul: Recovery - thrust fins, asymmetric and twisted rudders, vane wheels. They convert energy already in the water into thrust.
Drag and vortex reduction - rudder bulbs. They do not recover anything; they stop a loss from happening.

The bulb is often described loosely as recovering hub-vortex energy. The defensible statement is that it suppresses the vortex and restores pressure behind the boss. Say that and the point is safe either way.
Describing an asymmetric rudder as a rudder offset to one side of the centreline. The asymmetry is in the section and the twist about the shaft line, matching the opposite swirl above and below.
Saying the Grim vane wheel is geared to or driven by the shaft. It is entirely free-running; there is no mechanical connection, and that is the whole point.
Making the vane wheel the same diameter as the propeller. It is larger, and it must be, because the outer portion has to stand outside the race to act as a propeller.
Quoting a saving as a hard number. Every figure is conditional on the hull and the operating condition.
Adding the percentages of several devices together.
Ignoring manoeuvring. Anything bolted to a rudder changes the way she steers, and class will want to see the structure.

"Currently in use" in the stem. The Grim vane wheel is the odd one out - historically important, largely not in service. Say so rather than pretending it is common; an answer that quietly treats all four as current practice is weaker, not stronger.
Limb (d) is worth the same 4 marks as the others even though it is the least used. Do not short it.
The stem says the devices contribute to propulsion effectiveness, not to steering. Manoeuvring belongs in the closing judgement, not in place of the hydrodynamics.

questions.understand_first: A propeller does not convert all the power it is given into useful thrust. Some of what it leaves behind is axial - water thrown astern faster than it needs to be - and some is rotational: the race leaves the disc spinning, and that spin is wasted energy. Behind the propeller of a single-screw ship sits a large flat object in exactly that spinning race: the rudder. Every device in this question does one of two things with it - it either recovers some of the rotational energy and turns it into forward thrust, or it stops wasting more, by removing a vortex or a separation the rudder itself creates. Read the four limbs that way and they stop being four unrelated gadgets.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the rudder-efficiency question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the losses are - then the four printed limbs in order: (a) thrust fins, (b) asymmetric and twisted rudders, (c) rudder bulbs, (d) Grim vane wheels - then the management judgement on whether a claimed gain is real on this ship.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner prints 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. The four blocks must be equal, and the surrounding material has to be paid for out of the same 16 marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the rotational loss, and why does it matter here?
retrieval_cards.answer: The propeller leaves its race spinning as well as moving astern. That swirl is energy already paid for and thrown away - of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power on a single-screw ship. The rudder stands directly in it, which is why the rudder region is where these devices work.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single idea behind all four devices. Knowing it lets you reconstruct any of them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a rudder thrust fin produce thrust without power?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a horizontal foil on the rudder inside the propeller race. The race is rotating, so the flow meets the fin at an angle of attack without the fin being turned. The fin develops lift, and because the oncoming flow is inclined the lift vector tilts forward; its horizontal component is thrust.
retrieval_cards.why: The mechanism is the mark. Describing the fin's shape without the inclined-lift argument earns very little.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What exactly is asymmetric about an asymmetric rudder?
retrieval_cards.answer: The section and the twist about the shaft line, not the position. The propeller race strikes the upper half of the rudder from one side and the lower half from the other, so the leading edge is twisted in opposite senses above and below the shaft to align each half with the swirl it actually meets.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest error is to describe a rudder offset to one side of the centreline. That is a different thing entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a rudder bulb recover energy or reduce loss?
retrieval_cards.answer: Properly, it reduces loss. It suppresses the hub vortex and gives the flow a body to close around instead of separating behind a bare boss, restoring pressure there. It is often described loosely as recovering hub-vortex energy; the safe formulation is suppression and pressure recovery.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the one device in the four that is not a recovery device, and saying so shows you understand the mechanism rather than the marketing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain how a Grim vane wheel works.
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a freely rotating wheel aft of and coaxial with the propeller, larger in diameter, with no mechanical connection to the shaft. Its inner portion stands inside the propeller race and acts as a turbine, extracting energy from the swirl and driving the wheel round; its outer portion stands outside the race in clean water and acts as a propeller, converting that energy into additional thrust over a larger disc.
retrieval_cards.why: One blade doing two jobs at two radii is the whole idea, and it is what distinguishes the vane wheel from every other device on the list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must a vane wheel be larger in diameter than the propeller?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because its outer portion has to stand outside the propeller race to work as a propeller in undisturbed water. If the wheel were the same diameter, the whole blade would sit in the slipstream and there would be no propeller portion to return the extracted energy as thrust.
retrieval_cards.why: A favourite oral follow-up, and it tests whether the turbine-plus-propeller split has actually been understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A maker offers a 4 per cent saving from a rudder thrust fin. What do you ask before agreeing?
retrieval_cards.answer: In what condition was the 4 per cent measured - draught, speed, loading - and was it model scale or full scale, with what scale correction? How does it behave at our actual operating profile rather than at the design point? What else is already fitted, since devices interact and savings do not simply add? What does class require for the attachment and its structure, and what is the effect on manoeuvring?
retrieval_cards.why: This is the management-level mark. Anyone can recite the mechanism; the Class I candidate interrogates the claim.

blocks.h: 1. Adoption is not entry into force

blocks.p: A convention is adopted either by the competent IMO organ - the Assembly, MSC, MEPC or Legal Committee - or by a diplomatic conference. Adoption settles the text and does no more: it binds no State, and an adopted convention may never enter into force at all. The text is then opened for signature and deposited with the Secretary-General of IMO as depositary.

blocks.h: 2. How a State expresses consent to be bound

blocks.p: Between adoption and entry into force sits the step that actually matters: each State must express its consent to be bound, by one of three routes -

ul: signature alone, where the treaty so provides or the negotiating States so agreed;
signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, which is the normal course for multilateral conventions;
accession, where the State did not sign within the signature period.

blocks.p: In the second and third cases the State is bound only on depositing a formal instrument with the depositary, who records it, counts it towards the entry into force condition, and notifies all other States.

blocks.h: 3. The two terms the question names

blocks.p: (ii) Signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval. The State signs, but the signature does not bind it; it indicates an intention to proceed. The State becomes a party only on later depositing an instrument of ratification. Its modern purpose is to give the State time to enact the necessary domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements before committing internationally. Acceptance and approval are the same act under less formal names, used where a constitution does not demand the fuller procedure: VCLT Article 14(2) provides that consent is expressed by acceptance or approval under conditions similar to those which apply to ratification. In legal effect the three are identical.

(i) Accession. The means by which a State becomes party to a treaty it did not sign - because the signature period has closed, or because it was not a negotiating State. It is a single step: no prior signature, simply deposit of an instrument of accession, permitted by VCLT Article 15 where the treaty so provides. Once deposited it has exactly the same legal effect as ratification. The difference is the route, not the destination.

blocks.h: 4. The entry into force provision, and why it matters

blocks.p: Every convention contains a final clause fixing entry into force, normally a threshold of acceptances plus a waiting period. Its importance is fourfold:

ul: it prevents an instrument binding a handful of States while the rest operate to another standard, which would distort competition;
it fixes a certain date from which obligations, surveys and certificates run, so Administrations, recognised organisations, owners and yards all work to one deadline;
it provides the interval in which flag States legislate, class develops rules, and industry builds or retrofits;
it gives legitimacy - a convention in force across most world tonnage can be enforced through port State control against ships of non-parties, which is what makes no more favourable treatment work.

blocks.h: 5. Conventions of an important technical nature

blocks.p: For a convention of important technical nature - one dictating construction, equipment or operation - States observe a stiffer double condition: a number of States and a percentage of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping. A count of States alone could be satisfied by many small registries while the major fleets stayed outside, leaving a convention in force on paper and irrelevant at sea.

ul: SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, requiring not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping; in force 25 May 1980.
The 1978 MARPOL Protocol - in force twelve months after not less than fifteen States constituting not less than fifty per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage had become Parties.

blocks.p: Older conventions typically required two-thirds of contracting States, which occasionally meant more acceptances were needed to bring an instrument into force than to amend it.

blocks.h: 6. Keeping the convention current once in force

blocks.p: A technical convention is worthless if it cannot keep pace, and explicit acceptance failed on exactly that point: amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never received enough acceptances and none entered into force.

IMO's answer was the tacit acceptance procedure, used in SOLAS 1974, MARPOL and the collision regulations. It reverses the default: an amendment to the technical annexes is deemed accepted on a specified date unless objections are received beforehand from an agreed number of Parties. For SOLAS 1974 an amendment is deemed accepted at the end of two years from communication to Contracting Governments, unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments, or by Governments whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage. Amendments now enter into force typically within 18 to 24 months.

The sequence can be seen running at this very sitting. Under MARPOL article 16(2)(a) the Secretary-General circulated the draft revised Annex VI on 11 April 2025 for consideration with a view to adoption at an extraordinary session under article 16(2)(b), (c) and (d). Circulated, therefore, but not yet adopted - and still not adopted on the day this paper was sat. Finally, once in force internationally each flag State must still give the instrument domestic effect, in India through the Merchant Shipping Act and the rules made under it, and it is that domestic instrument which is enforced against the ship.

blocks.h: Four words that are not synonyms

blocks.p: Adoption settles the text. Signature may or may not bind, depending on what the treaty says. Ratification, acceptance, approval or accession is the act that binds the State, and it binds on deposit, not on decision at home. Entry into force is when the instrument starts to operate, for those States and thereafter for later parties. Candidates use all four as though they meant the same thing, and the whole question is built on their not meaning the same thing.

blocks.h: The same problem exists in domestic law

blocks.p: This is worth noticing because this paper tests it twice. An Indian Act is passed, then receives assent, then commences on a date appointed by notification - and it is not law until it commences. That is structurally the same three-stage problem as adoption, ratification and entry into force. Q9 of this paper turns on it: at this sitting the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 was still the Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024, introduced in December 2024 and passed by neither House; it was assented in August 2025 and did not commence until March 2026. Revising Q2 and Q9 together is far more efficient than revising them apart, because they are one idea in two settings.

blocks.h: Why tonnage and not just a headcount

blocks.p: The double condition looks like bureaucratic detail and is in fact the most commercially significant sentence in the answer. A safety convention that binds fifty small registries and none of the major fleets creates a competitive distortion rather than a safety improvement: compliant ships carry the cost and non-compliant ships take the trade. Requiring a percentage of world gross tonnage ensures the instrument binds the fleet that actually carries the cargo, which is what then makes port State control and no more favourable treatment effective against the remainder.

blocks.h: 1. (a) Port of refuge - what it is and why a ship puts in

blocks.p: A port of refuge is a port or place, not the intended destination, into which a ship deviates because she cannot safely continue the voyage. The usual causes are heavy weather damage, grounding or collision damage, fire, a shift of cargo, main engine or steering failure, or a medical emergency. Putting in is a deviation, and in insurance terms that is the first thing to say about it: a deviation not justified by the policy discharges the insurer from liability from the moment of deviation, but a deviation reasonably made for the safety of the ship or of life is excused, as is one made to save human life or to secure necessary assistance.

The regulatory backdrop should be stated correctly, because it is the point on which most answers are out of date. Guidance is given by the IMO Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance, resolution A.1184(33) adopted on 6 December 2023, which by its operative paragraph 4 revokes the earlier resolution A.949(23) of 2003. The Guidelines are recommendatory, and their central premise is blunt: a coastal State is under no obligation in international law to grant a place of refuge. It must weigh the ship's need against the protection of its own coastline, which is why refusal or delay is a real commercial risk and not a theoretical one.

This is where the insurance content lies. If the ship put in for the common safety of ship and cargo, the entry is a general average act within Rule A, and the York-Antwerp Rules then allow the resulting expenditure as general average - to be shared rateably by ship, cargo and freight according to contributory values:

ul: Rule X allows the port charges of entering the port or place of refuge and of leaving it, and the cost of handling, discharging, storing and reloading cargo, fuel and stores, where that handling is necessary for the common safety or to allow damage caused by sacrifice or accident to be repaired.
Rule XI allows the wages and maintenance of master, officers and crew, and the fuel and stores consumed, during the prolongation of the voyage occasioned by putting in or being detained there.

blocks.p: Two qualifications carry the marks. First, the allowance depends on the purpose: expenditure incurred for the common safety is general average, whereas repairs and costs relating only to the ship's own accidental damage are particular average on the ship and fall on her owner and his hull underwriter alone. A single call at a port of refuge routinely generates both, and the average adjuster's task is to separate them. Second, general average is not affected by fault as to entitlement: the party at fault may still claim contribution, leaving the other parties to their separate remedies for the breach - which is what keeps the adjustment moving. The practical consequence for the ship is that average security - an average bond from cargo receivers and an average guarantee from their underwriters - must be collected before cargo is released.

Particular average is a partial loss of the subject-matter insured, caused by a peril insured against, which is not a general average loss. Its three defining features are that it is accidental and not deliberate; that it affects a particular interest only - hull, or one parcel of cargo; and that it lies where it falls. There is no sharing: the owner of the damaged property bears it, and recovers from his own underwriter if the loss was proximately caused by a peril insured against, subject to the deductible or franchise in his policy. Heavy weather damage to a hatch cover, or seawater damage to one hold of cargo, is particular average.

General average arises from a general average act, and Rule A defines it exactly: "there is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure." The loss is then shared rateably by all the interests saved, in proportion to their contributory values, through an adjustment prepared by an average adjuster. Jettison of cargo to refloat, flooding a hold to fight a fire, and the cost of engaging salvors are the standard examples.
Set out as a contrast, the distinction is clean:

ul: Cause - particular average is accidental; general average is intentional.
Purpose - general average is for the common safety of the whole adventure; particular average has no purpose at all.
Incidence - particular average lies where it falls; general average is contributed to by everyone saved.
Machinery - particular average is a claim on the assured's own policy; general average requires an adjustment, average security, and contribution from parties who may have suffered no damage at all.
The extraordinary requirement - ordinary use of the ship, however hard, is not a sacrifice. This is where most general average arguments are actually fought.

blocks.p: A total loss is either actual or constructive. There is an actual total loss where the subject-matter insured is destroyed; or is so damaged that it ceases to be a thing of the kind insured - cement set hard in the hold, a ship burnt to a shell; or where the assured is irretrievably deprived of it, as by capture or by a sinking beyond recovery. To these the law adds the missing ship: where a ship is missing and no news of her is received after a reasonable time, an actual total loss may be presumed. On an actual total loss the assured claims the full sum insured and no notice of abandonment is required, because there is nothing left to abandon.

blocks.h: 6. (c) Constructive total loss and notice of abandonment

blocks.p: The examiner's printed words are "Total Loss and Constructive Loss"; the term of art is constructive total loss, and using it correctly is itself worth something. There is a constructive total loss where the subject-matter is reasonably abandoned because its actual total loss appears unavoidable, or because it could not be preserved from actual total loss without an expenditure which would exceed its value when that expenditure had been incurred. In practice it arises in three ways: the ship is so damaged that the cost of repair would exceed her repaired value; the assured is deprived of possession and is unlikely to recover her, or the cost of recovery would exceed her value; or cargo is so damaged that the cost of repairing and forwarding it would exceed its value on arrival.

The machinery matters as much as the test. To claim for a constructive total loss the assured must give notice of abandonment to the underwriter, with reasonable diligence after receiving reliable information of the loss; if he does not, the loss can be treated only as a partial loss. Notice may be waived by the underwriter, and is unnecessary where there would be no possibility of benefit to him. If the abandonment is accepted it is irrevocable, the acceptance conclusively admits liability and the sufficiency of the notice, and the underwriter takes over the assured's interest in whatever remains, together with proprietary rights incidental to it - which is how underwriters come to own wrecks. The assured is not bound to abandon: he may elect to treat the loss as partial instead. To these two legal categories the market adds a third, purely commercial one, the compromised or arranged total loss, where liability is disputed or the tests are marginal and the claim is settled at an agreed figure without either side conceding the point.

Three limbs and no printed marks between them, so treat them as roughly equal and give each the same weight. "Short notes" is an instruction about length, not about depth: the examiner still wants a definition, the legal test and the consequence. Two route steps per limb - what it is, then who pays - keeps the notes short without making them thin.

blocks.p: The IMO guidance on places of refuge is resolution A.1184(33), adopted 6 December 2023. Its operative paragraph 4 revokes A.949(23), the 2003 resolution that nearly every circulating note set still quotes. A.949(23) had already been revoked for eighteen months when this paper was sat, so citing it is not merely dated - it is wrong for this sitting. If you cannot remember the number, write "the current IMO Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance" and give their substance; that is safe, whereas a confident wrong number is not.

ul: Answering limb (a) as a seamanship or SAR question. The stem says with reference to Marine Insurance: the substance is deviation, general average and who pays.
Forgetting that a single port of refuge call generates both general average and particular average, and that separating them is the adjuster's job.
Saying a coastal State must admit a ship in distress. It must not refuse arbitrarily, but it is under no obligation to grant a place of refuge.
Defining general average without the words extraordinary, intentionally, reasonably and common safety. Each is load-bearing.
Treating constructive total loss as "badly damaged". The test is economic - unavoidable actual total loss, or cost of preservation exceeding value.
Omitting notice of abandonment. Without it the assured recovers only for a partial loss, and that is the whole practical consequence of the limb.
Requiring notice of abandonment for an actual total loss. None is needed.
"Constructive Loss" is printed loosely in the stem. The term of art is constructive total loss, and using it correctly shows you know the category rather than the phrase.

Limb (b) overlaps Q6 of this same paper, which is general average proper. Here give the distinction; save the essential features and the refloating analysis for Q6. Repeating Q6 in Q3 wastes the time, not the marks.
General average entitlement survives fault. The party at fault may still claim contribution; the others are left to their separate remedies. Saying the opposite is a common and confident error.

retrieval_cards.answer: Those incurred for the common safety: the port charges in and out, and the handling, discharge, storage and reloading of cargo where necessary for the common safety or to allow the damage to be repaired, under Rule X; and crew wages and maintenance and stores consumed during the prolongation, under Rule XI. blocks.h: 1. The problem SCOPIC was written to cure

blocks.p: Salvage is no cure - no pay. Under the Salvage Convention 1989, in force 14 July 1996, the salvor earns a reward under Article 13 only if he saves property, and the reward cannot exceed the salved value. That is a poor bargain for a laden tanker aground on a falling tide with no realisable property value but an enormous pollution risk. Article 14 was the Convention's answer: where the vessel threatened damage to the environment and the Article 13 reward was less, the salvor recovers special compensation equal to his expenses, increasable by up to 30 per cent and, if the tribunal thinks it fair and just, up to 100 per cent of expenses.

In practice Article 14 failed the people it was written for, for four reasons. It required proof of a "threat of damage to the environment", which was itself litigated. "Expenses" was judicially confined to out-of-pocket cost and a fair rate for equipment and personnel, with no profit element. Everything was assessed after the event by arbitration, so the salvor financed a long operation on an uncertain outcome. And there was no security mechanism to make sure he was eventually paid.

The Special Compensation P&I Clause is a contractual clause agreed between the International Salvage Union, the International Group of P&I Clubs and property underwriters, first effective 1 August 1999 and revised since; the version current at this examination is SCOPIC 2020, in effect from 1 January 2020. It is supplementary to a Lloyd's Form salvage agreement and, once incorporated and invoked, it substitutes its own method of assessment for Article 14(1) to (4). It is not part of the Convention and not law: it works because the parties agree to it.

blocks.h: 3. How it answers each of the salvor's difficulties

ul: The threshold argument disappears. By sub-clause 2 the salvor may invoke SCOPIC by written notice at any time of his choosing, regardless of the circumstances and in particular regardless of whether there is a threat of damage to the environment. Assessment runs from the notice, so there is a real incentive to invoke early.

Remuneration becomes calculable, not litigable. Sub-clause 5 replaces "expenses" with a pre-agreed tariff for personnel, tugs, craft and portable equipment on a time-and-materials basis, plus out-of-pocket expenses, plus a standard bonus of 25 per cent of those rates. The bonus is the profit element the courts held Article 14 did not provide.

He is secured. By sub-clause 3(i) owners must provide a bank guarantee or P&I Club letter for US$3 million within 2 working days of the notice; the sum may be increased or reduced as the job develops. If it is not provided, sub-clause 4(i) lets the salvor withdraw from SCOPIC and revert to Article 14.

Facts are recorded as they happen. Sub-clause 12 provides for a Special Casualty Representative, appointed by the owners and attending the casualty, who reports on the salvage as it proceeds. An agreed contemporaneous record removes most of what arbitration used to be spent arguing about.

He is paid before final assessment. Sub-clause 8 requires 75 per cent of the excess of assessed SCOPIC remuneration over the Article 13 security to be paid within 1 month, with interest at US prime plus 1 per cent.

blocks.p: Two balancing provisions stop the clause being abused, and naming them is what separates a good answer from a recitation. By sub-clause 6(i) the Article 13 assessment continues, and SCOPIC remuneration is payable by the shipowner alone and only to the extent it exceeds the Article 13 award - so the salvor gets the better of the two, not both. And by sub-clause 7, if the Article 13 award turns out to be the greater, that award is discounted by 25 per cent of the difference. The salvor therefore pays for the safety net if it turns out he did not need it, which is what keeps SCOPIC for the cases it was meant for.

blocks.h: 4. (i) Disciplinary action against the master or crew

blocks.p: The right belongs to the flag State of the ship, or to the State of nationality of the person concerned - and to no one else. The authority is UNCLOS Article 97(1): in the event of a collision or any other incident of navigation concerning a ship on the high seas, involving the penal or disciplinary responsibility of the master or of any other person in the service of the ship, no penal or disciplinary proceedings may be instituted against such person except before the judicial or administrative authorities either of the flag State or of the State of which such person is a national.

The justification is the legal character of the high seas. No State has territorial sovereignty there, so the only connecting factors are the flag - the ship being subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the flag State under Article 92, whose duties of effective jurisdiction and control are set out in Article 94 - and the nationality of the individual. The rule is also a deliberate historical correction: it reverses the result of the Lotus case, in which a State was held entitled to try the officer of a foreign ship for a high-seas collision, and it was first put into treaty form in the Brussels Convention 1952 on Penal Jurisdiction in Matters of Collision. Article 97(3) completes the protection: no arrest or detention of the ship, even as a measure of investigation, may be ordered by any authorities other than those of the flag State.

Only the State which issued the certificate may cancel it. UNCLOS Article 97(2) is explicit: in disciplinary matters, only the State which issued a master's certificate or a certificate of competence or licence is competent, after due legal process, to pronounce the withdrawal of such certificates, even if the holder is not a national of that State.

This is a narrower rule than limb (i) and must not be merged with it. For proceedings generally there are two candidate States, flag or nationality; for withdrawal of a certificate there is exactly one, the issuing administration - and the closing words settle the case the examiner is really testing, where an officer holds the certificate of a State he is not a national of. Note also what is not restricted: the words are "withdrawal of such certificates". A flag State that has issued an endorsement recognising a foreign certificate may withdraw its own endorsement, and a port State may act against the ship under its own port State control powers. Neither cancels the certificate.

This limb is different in kind and the mark lies in saying so. Compensation is a matter of civil liability between the parties, not of a State's right to act, and UNCLOS Article 97 does not touch it. The applicable convention is the Collision Convention 1910 - the Brussels Convention for the unification of certain rules of law with respect to collisions between vessels - whose salient points are these:

ul: If the collision is accidental, or caused by force majeure, or its cause is left in doubt, the damages are borne by those who have suffered them.
If caused by the fault of one vessel, that vessel bears the loss.

If both are at fault, liability is in proportion to the degree of fault of each; where the degrees cannot be established, or the fault appears equal, liability is divided equally. This replaced the older English rule of equal division in every case of mutual fault.
There is no legal presumption of fault from the collision itself; fault must be proved.

For loss of life and personal injury the vessels at fault are jointly and severally liable to the victims, with a right of recourse between them; for property damage liability is only proportionate, so a cargo owner recovers from each ship only its share.

blocks.p: The forum is then a separate question, governed by the Brussels Convention 1952 on Civil Jurisdiction in Matters of Collision - broadly, the court of the defendant's residence or place of business, or where the vessel has been arrested or security given, or where the collision occurred if that was in a port or inland waters. In practice the claimant chooses by arresting the ship. Two riders complete the answer: the total payable may then be capped by the LLMC regime, and both Conventions apply only between States party to them, so the position turns on the ratifications of the two flag States - which this question does not identify. Where India is the forum, the collision provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, in force at this examination, give domestic effect.

The paper prints no marks between (a) and (b), so the safe reading is roughly half each, with limb (b)'s eight marks split three ways. That matters, because limb (b) has three printed sub-limbs and each needs a named State, a justification and a convention. An answer that discusses collision liability generally and never answers "which State" has not answered the question asked.

blocks.h: The one provision that answers two-thirds of limb (b)

blocks.p: UNCLOS Article 97. Sub-article (1) gives limb (i) - flag State or State of nationality. Sub-article (2) gives limb (ii) - only the issuing State, even for a non-national. Sub-article (3) gives the bonus point that no other State may even arrest the ship as a measure of investigation. If you learn one thing for this question, learn Article 97.

blocks.h: Keep the three limbs in different legal categories

ul: (i) is penal and disciplinary jurisdiction - a State punishing a person. UNCLOS restricts it to two States.
(ii) is a narrower disciplinary power - withdrawing a certificate. UNCLOS restricts it to one State, the issuer.
(iii) is civil liability - one shipowner paying another. UNCLOS says nothing about it; the 1910 Convention apportions it and the 1952 Convention decides where the case is heard.
Candidates lose marks by giving the same answer three times. The examiner has deliberately built a question where the answer narrows from (i) to (ii) and then changes category at (iii).
Saying the coastal State, or the State of the other ship, may prosecute. On the high seas neither may.
Saying the flag State may cancel any certificate. It may cancel the ones it issued, and its own endorsement of a foreign certificate - not the foreign certificate itself.
Treating compensation as a jurisdictional question with a single answer. It is a civil claim; the real questions are apportionment and forum.

Saying liability is always divided equally when both are at fault. That is the pre-1910 rule; the Convention apportions by degree of fault, and divides equally only where the degrees cannot be established.
In limb (a), describing SCOPIC as part of the Salvage Convention. It is a contractual clause supplementary to a Lloyd's Form.
Saying SCOPIC pays in addition to the Article 13 award. It is payable only to the extent it exceeds it.
"On the high seas" is doing all the work in limb (b). Inside a territorial sea the coastal State's criminal jurisdiction is engaged and the answer changes completely. Say why the location matters.

"With justification" is an instruction, not decoration. Each sub-limb needs the reason - exclusive flag State jurisdiction, the issuing administration's competence, the civil character of a compensation claim.
The 25 per cent in SCOPIC appears twice with opposite effects: the bonus on the tariff and the discount on the Article 13 award. Mixing them up is a common and visible error.
The stem asks how SCOPIC solves "the difficulties of salvors" - so the Article 14 problems must be stated before the cure, or the cure has nothing to bite on.
Your ship collides with a foreign vessel on the high seas. Can the other State detain you for investigation?
You hold an Indian certificate and serve on a Panama-flagged ship. Who can take your certificate away?
When would you advise the master to invoke SCOPIC?
Why would a salvor not invoke SCOPIC immediately?
Both ships are equally to blame and a seafarer dies. Who does his family sue?

blocks.p: Two numbers carry limb (b): 97 for punishment, 1910 for money. Within 97, count down - two States may prosecute, one may withdraw a certificate, one may arrest. For limb (a), the four Article 14 problems and the four SCOPIC cures pair off: threshold to free invocation, no profit to the 25 per cent bonus, late assessment to the tariff and the SCR, no security to the US$3 million letter.

questions.understand_first: The two limbs look unrelated and are joined by one idea: who pays, and who may punish, when a casualty happens outside anybody's territory. Limb (a) is about paying a salvor when the ordinary no-cure-no-pay bargain would leave him unpaid for work society wants done. Limb (b) is about the opposite reflex - the instinct that after a collision somebody must prosecute - and the answer is that on the high seas the number of States entitled to do so is deliberately very small. Keep penal and disciplinary jurisdiction (limbs i and ii, which UNCLOS restricts) rigidly apart from civil liability (limb iii, which it does not touch at all).

retrieval_cards.prompt: After a high-seas collision, which States may take disciplinary proceedings against the master?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only two: the flag State of the ship, or the State of which the master is a national. UNCLOS Article 97(1). And by Article 97(3) no authority other than the flag State may arrest or detain the ship, even as a measure of investigation.
retrieval_cards.why: The instinct that the other ship's State or a nearby coastal State can prosecute is exactly what Article 97 was written to stop, reversing the Lotus decision.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who may cancel a certificate of competency after a high-seas collision?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only the State which issued it, after due legal process, and expressly so even if the holder is not a national of that State. UNCLOS Article 97(2).
retrieval_cards.why: It is narrower than Article 97(1): two States may prosecute, but only one may take the certificate away.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is limb (iii), compensation, different in kind from the first two?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it is civil, not penal or disciplinary. It is a claim between shipowners, not a State exercising a power, so UNCLOS Article 97 does not apply. The Collision Convention 1910 apportions the liability and the Brussels Convention 1952 decides where the claim is heard.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner narrows the answer from two States to one and then changes category. Answering all three the same way is the commonest failure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the Collision Convention 1910 apportion liability?
retrieval_cards.answer: If the collision is accidental, caused by force majeure, or its cause is in doubt, each bears his own loss. If one vessel is at fault she bears it. If both are at fault, liability is in proportion to the degree of fault, and only where the degrees cannot be established is it divided equally. There is no presumption of fault. For death and personal injury the vessels are jointly and severally liable; for property damage only proportionately.
retrieval_cards.why: The proportionate rule replaced the old equal-division rule, and the split between personal injury and property is the detail that shows the Convention has actually been read.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is SCOPIC and what does it do to Article 14?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Special Compensation P&I Clause, agreed between the International Salvage Union, the International Group of P&I Clubs and property underwriters and first effective 1 August 1999; SCOPIC 2020 is the current version. It is a contractual clause supplementary to a Lloyd's Form salvage agreement, and once incorporated and invoked it substitutes its own method of assessment for Article 14(1) to (4).
retrieval_cards.why: It is not part of the Convention and not law. It works because the parties agree to it, and saying so is the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: SCOPIC contains two figures of 25 per cent. What are they?
retrieval_cards.answer: A standard bonus of 25 per cent added to the Appendix A tariff rates, which supplies the profit element Article 14 lacked; and a discount of 25 per cent of the difference applied to the Article 13 award where that award exceeds the assessed SCOPIC remuneration, which discourages invoking SCOPIC when it was not needed.
retrieval_cards.why: They pull in opposite directions - one pays the salvor more, the other pays him less - and confusing them is a visible error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a salvor who invokes SCOPIC get both SCOPIC remuneration and the Article 13 award?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. By sub-clause 6(i) the Article 13 assessment continues, but SCOPIC remuneration is payable by the owners of the vessel alone and only to the extent that it exceeds the total Article 13 award payable by all salved interests. He receives the better of the two, not the sum of them.
retrieval_cards.why: This, with the 25 per cent discount, is what keeps SCOPIC a safety net rather than a bonus, and it is the part candidates most often get wrong.

blocks.h: 1. What the Convention is, and the bargain it strikes

blocks.p: The Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims, 1976 - the LLMC - was adopted on 19 November 1976 and entered into force on 1 December 1986. Its 1996 Protocol, in force 13 May 2004, substantially raised the limits and introduced a tacit acceptance procedure for raising them again; amendments adopted under it in 2012 took effect on 8 June 2015. India gives effect to the regime through Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, which is the statute in force at this examination.

The Convention's purpose is to allow a shipowner to limit his total liability arising out of a single occurrence to a fund calculated by reference to the tonnage of the ship, irrespective of the actual amount of the loss. The policy behind it is commercial rather than moral: maritime adventure exposes an owner to potential liabilities out of all proportion to the value of the vessel and the freight, and without a cap the risk would be uninsurable at an acceptable premium. The Convention therefore buys certainty and insurability for the owner, and in exchange gives the claimant a fund that is almost unbreakable but almost automatic: by Article 2 the listed claims are subject to limitation "whatever the basis of liability may be", so the owner does not have to prove absence of fault to rely on it.

blocks.h: 2. The two heads of claim under Article 6

blocks.p: Article 6 sets the general limits, and it does so under two separate heads, each with its own fund:

ol: claims for loss of life or personal injury; and
any other claims - in practice the property head, covering damage to ships, harbour works, basins, waterways and aids to navigation, loss of or damage to property on board, and consequential loss.

blocks.p: The two funds are distinct and are not interchangeable: a property claimant cannot reach into the personal-injury fund. Their significance is the deliberate priority given to life - the life and injury limit is set materially higher, and where that fund is insufficient the balance of those claims ranks rateably with property claims against the other fund. Both limits rise in steps with tonnage.

One refinement should be stated to show precision. Claims by passengers of a ship for loss of life or personal injury are dealt with separately, under Article 7, by a limit calculated on the number of passengers the ship is certified to carry rather than on tonnage. So the two heads asked for are the Article 6 heads; the passenger limit sits alongside them and is not one of them.

blocks.h: 3. Who may limit - and what cannot be limited at all

blocks.p: Article 1 answers the question directly. The persons entitled to limit are shipowners and salvors, and the Convention defines both widely:

ul: "Shipowner" means the owner, charterer, manager and operator of a seagoing ship. A bareboat or time charterer may therefore limit in his own right.

A "salvor" is any person rendering services in direct connexion with salvage operations. This was added deliberately in 1976 to close the gap exposed where a salvage master working in the water, and not from a vessel, was held unable to limit under the earlier regime.
Any person for whose act, neglect or default the shipowner or salvor is responsible - master, crew, servants and agents - may invoke the same limits.
An insurer of liability for claims subject to limitation is entitled to the benefits of the Convention to the same extent as the assured, which is what makes direct action against the club workable.

blocks.p: The counterpart is Article 3: certain claims are excepted from limitation altogether. They include claims for salvage and for contribution in general average, oil pollution claims falling within the CLC regime, nuclear damage claims, and claims by the servants of the shipowner or salvor whose contracts of service are governed by a law that does not permit limitation. Note the position of salvage on both sides of the line: a salvor may limit his own liability, but a claim for salvage cannot be limited against.

Plaintiff. The party who commences a civil action, asserting a right and asking the court for a remedy, and who carries the burden of proving his case on the balance of probabilities. In modern English procedure the term has largely been replaced by "claimant"; in Indian civil procedure the plaintiff is the party who files the plaint. In a limitation context he is typically the cargo owner, the injured seafarer or the port authority claiming against the fund.

Defendant. The party against whom the action is brought, who must answer the claim and who may raise defences, set-offs and counterclaims. In this context he is typically the shipowner, and it is the defendant who invokes limitation. The distinction matters procedurally: limitation is not something the court applies of its own motion, it is relied on by the party sued, and in most jurisdictions it is pursued by constituting a limitation fund and seeking a decree limiting liability.

blocks.h: 5. Privity - and why it is the old test

blocks.p: Privity means knowledge of and concurrence in the act or condition complained of. A person is privy to something if he knew of it and assented to it, expressly or by turning a blind eye - it is more than negligence and less than intention, and it is personal to him, not something imputed from the acts of his servants.

Its importance is historical and it should be presented that way. Under the regime that preceded the LLMC, an owner lost his right to limit if the loss occurred with his "actual fault or privity". That test was comparatively easy for a claimant to satisfy: proof that the owner knew the ship was undermanned or that a defect had been reported to the office could break the limit, and limitation actions were routinely fought on it.

Article 4 of the LLMC deliberately replaced it with a far harder test. A person loses the right to limit only if the loss resulted from his personal act or omission, committed with the intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result. The burden is on the claimant, the conduct must be personal - the alter ego of the company, not the master - and recklessness must be coupled with actual knowledge of the probable consequence. That is why the modern limit is described as almost unbreakable, and it is the single most important thing to say about privity: the word belongs to the old law, and quoting it as the current test is the error the examiner is looking for.

Unlimited liability is liability that is not capped by any limitation regime, so that the claimant may recover the full amount of his proven loss however large. Under this Convention it arises by three distinct routes, and a good answer separates them: first, where the Article 4 conduct test is satisfied, so the right to limit is lost; second, where the claim is excepted by Article 3, so the right never applied to it - salvage and general average contribution are the everyday examples; and third, where the Convention does not govern at all, because the forum State is not party to it or the liability arises under a separate regime with its own rules. The practical consequence is the one the Chief Engineer meets: it is the owner's own knowledge and decisions - what the office was told, what was recorded, what was authorised - that put the limit at risk, and that is why defect reporting and the ship-to-shore record matter far beyond the engineering department.

The paper prints 8 + 8, so limb (b) - four words - is worth exactly as much as the whole of the Convention in limb (a). Candidates routinely write three-quarters of a page on LLMC and four lines of dictionary definitions, and lose half the question. Three steps each side, and limb (b) treated as law rather than vocabulary, is the shape that scores.

blocks.h: The thread that ties the two limbs together

blocks.p: The examiner has not asked two unrelated things. Privity is the old test for breaking limitation and Article 4 is the new one; unlimited liability is what happens when the limit breaks; and plaintiff and defendant are the two sides of the fight over whether it breaks. Say that explicitly and the answer reads as one piece of law rather than as an essay followed by a glossary.

ul: The two heads under Article 6 are loss of life or personal injury and any other claims. Say "any other claims", not "property damage" alone - the second head is residual and wider than property.
Two separate funds. A property claimant cannot reach the life fund.
Life ranks higher, and the balance of unsatisfied life claims ranks rateably against the property fund.
Passengers are Article 7 and are separate. Naming them as one of the two heads is wrong; naming them as a distinct additional limit is a mark.
Do not quote SDR figures unless asked. If you do, you must first say which instrument binds the State - the unamended 1976 Convention gives materially lower figures than the amended 1996 Protocol.
Treating limitation as a denial of liability. It is an admission of liability with a cap.
Saying only "the shipowner" can limit. Article 1 includes charterer, manager and operator, and separately salvors, servants and the liability insurer.
Giving "actual fault or privity" as the current test for breaking the limit. It is the superseded test.
Forgetting that salvage and general average contribution cannot be limited against, while a salvor himself may limit.

"Two heads of claims" is precise language and the examiner is testing whether you know that Article 6 has exactly two. Listing four or five categories of claim from Article 2 answers a different question.
"Who can limit" invites the Article 1 list, not a discussion of when limitation is lost. Keep Article 4 for the privity limb, where it earns marks twice.

The shipowner does not say he is not liable; he accepts liability and says that the total he must pay for one occurrence is capped by a figure calculated from his ship's tonnage, whatever the actual loss was. retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the LLMC question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 what the Convention is and the bargain it strikes; 2 the two heads of claim under Article 6; 3 who may limit under Article 1, and what Article 3 excepts. Limb (b): 4 plaintiff and defendant; 5 privity as the old test against Article 4 as the new one; 6 unlimited liability by its three routes.
retrieval_cards.why: The paper prints 8 + 8, so limb (b) needs three real steps of its own. Treating it as a glossary throws away half the marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two heads of claim under Article 6?
retrieval_cards.answer: Claims for loss of life or personal injury, and any other claims. They are two separate funds and are not interchangeable; the life and injury limit is higher, and the balance of unsatisfied life claims ranks rateably against the property fund. Passenger claims are separate again, under Article 7.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for exactly two. Listing categories of claim from Article 2, or promoting the passenger limit into the pair, answers a different question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who is entitled to limit under Article 1?
retrieval_cards.answer: Shipowners and salvors. "Shipowner" means the owner, charterer, manager and operator of a seagoing ship; a "salvor" is any person rendering services in direct connexion with salvage operations. Persons for whose act, neglect or default the shipowner or salvor is responsible may invoke the same limits, and a liability insurer is entitled to the benefit of the Convention to the same extent as the assured.
retrieval_cards.why: The width of the definition is the mark. "The shipowner" alone misses the charterer, the salvor and the insurer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is "actual fault or privity" the test for breaking limitation today?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is the superseded pre-LLMC test. Article 4 replaced it with a much harder one: the claimant must show the loss resulted from the person's personal act or omission, committed with the intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the trap the examiner set by putting "privity" in the list. Defining it correctly and then dating it correctly earns twice.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define privity.
retrieval_cards.answer: Knowledge of and concurrence in the act or condition complained of - the person knew of it and assented to it, expressly or by turning a blind eye. It is more than negligence and less than intention, and it is personal to the owner rather than imputed from the acts of his servants.
retrieval_cards.why: The personal character of privity is what carries over into Article 4, where the conduct must again be personal.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the three routes to unlimited liability.
retrieval_cards.answer: One, the Article 4 conduct test is satisfied and the right to limit is lost. Two, the claim is excepted by Article 3 - salvage, general average contribution, CLC oil pollution, nuclear damage, certain servants' claims - so the right never applied to it. Three, no limitation Convention governs the forum State or the particular liability at all.
retrieval_cards.why: Separating "lost", "never applied" and "not governed" is what turns a definition into an answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A salvor may limit, yet salvage cannot be limited against. Explain.
retrieval_cards.answer: The two propositions operate on different sides of the claim. Article 1 makes the salvor a person entitled to limit his own liability - for example if he damages the casualty. Article 3 excepts claims for salvage from limitation, so when the salvor is the claimant, the owner cannot cap what he must pay for the salvage award.
retrieval_cards.why: Stated together without that separation the answer reads as self-contradictory, and the gate records it as the technical ambiguity of this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statute gave effect to limitation at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958. That Act was in force throughout June 2025 and was repealed only with effect from 15 March 2026, so the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 must not be named in an answer to this paper.

blocks.h: 1. a) What a general average act is

blocks.p: The statement in the question is correct, and the features are not a matter of opinion: they are drawn from the definition itself. Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules provides that there is a general average act 'when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure'.

Note first how the Rules apply. They are not law: they take effect by incorporation into the contract of carriage - the bill of lading or charterparty - and the Rule of Interpretation then makes them apply 'to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith'. In India the concept is also recognised in the Marine Insurance Act 1963.
Every phrase of Rule A is doing work, and each yields one essential feature:

ol: Extraordinary. The sacrifice or expenditure must be outside the ordinary performance of the contract of carriage. Fuel burned on a normal passage, or wear on machinery in ordinary service, is not extraordinary however costly.

Intentional and voluntary. The loss must be deliberately incurred. Cargo washed overboard by a sea is accidental and lies where it falls; cargo jettisoned by decision is a sacrifice. This is the single feature that most sharply separates general from particular average.
Reasonable. Reinforced by the Rule Paramount, which overrides everything else: 'In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred.'
Peril. There must be real danger - not necessarily immediate, but genuine and substantial, and more than the ordinary risk of the sea.

Common safety and common adventure. The act must be for the benefit of the whole adventure, not one interest alone, and there must be more than one interest at risk. A ship in ballast with no cargo on board has no common adventure and can have no general average.
Preservation of property. The purpose must be to preserve the property from that peril. Success matters: there must be something saved to contribute.

blocks.h: 3. The lettered rules that qualify the definition

ul: Rule C - only losses which are the direct consequence of the general average act are allowed. It expressly excludes demurrage, loss of market, loss caused by delay and any indirect loss whatsoever, and excludes environmental damage and the consequences of escaping pollutants.

Rule D - rights to contribution are not affected even though the event was due to the fault of one of the parties, without prejudice to any remedies or defences in respect of that fault. So the adjustment proceeds first, and blame is fought separately.
Rule E - the onus of proof is on the party claiming, who must give notice in writing to the average adjuster and supply particulars, generally within twelve months.

blocks.h: 4. How the loss is shared, and what general average is not

blocks.p: Under Rule A.2 the sacrifice is borne by the different contributing interests - ship, cargo and freight at risk - rateably in proportion to their values at the termination of the adventure. The adjustment is prepared by an average adjuster, and security is taken before cargo is released, normally an average bond from the receiver and an average guarantee from the cargo underwriter.

Two distinctions complete the picture. General average is not particular average: particular average is accidental damage, falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared. And general average is not insurance: it is a rule of contribution between the parties to the adventure, which predates marine insurance entirely, though the contribution is in practice recoverable under the policy.

blocks.h: 5. b) The refloating scenario - the rule that governs it

blocks.p: This situation is dealt with expressly, and by a rule written for exactly these facts. Rule VII, 'Damage to Machinery and Boilers', provides:

'Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.'

blocks.h: 6. Applying it - when the damage is allowed, and when it is not

blocks.p: Yes, the burnt bearings can be allowed in general average - provided four things are shown.

ol: The ship was ashore. She was aground, so the first condition is met on the facts given.

She was in a position of peril. This must be established, not assumed. A vessel lying safely aground on soft mud in fine weather, in no danger and awaiting the tide, is not in peril; one working on a hard bottom, or exposed to weather, tide or the risk of breaking her back, is. This is the condition on which the claim will actually turn.

The machinery was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety. Running the engine ahead and astern to shake her off is precisely that - a deliberate act directed at the safety of the whole adventure, not a routine manoeuvre.

The damage arose at the risk of such damage. The master must have accepted the risk of damaging the engine as the price of refloating. Working an engine hard, astern and ahead, against a grounded hull is known to overload the bearings, and it is that knowing acceptance that makes the loss a sacrifice rather than an accident.

blocks.p: The damage then satisfies Rule A as well: it is extraordinary (not ordinary service), intentional (the engine was deliberately worked in a way likely to damage it), reasonable if refloating was a sensible response, and directed at the common safety. It is also the direct consequence of the act, as Rule C requires. Under Rule D it makes no difference to the right of contribution that the grounding may have been somebody's fault.

The converse must be stated, because it is the trap. Rule VII closes with an absolute prohibition: where the ship is afloat, damage from working the propelling machinery is 'in no circumstances' allowed. So if she had already come off and the bearings burnt while manoeuvring clear, or if she were merely touching and not in peril, the same physical damage would be particular average - the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy and not shared with cargo. The engine damage is identical; the legal answer is opposite; and what decides it is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked.

Limb (a) is a 'discuss the statement' question, and the highest-scoring way to discuss it is to show that the essential features are not a list somebody invented but the clauses of the Rule A definition read one at a time. That converts a memory answer into an analytical one. Limb (b) is worth the same 8 marks and is decided by a single rule, so the answer must quote Rule VII, apply its four conditions to the facts, and then state the converse. An answer that says 'yes, it is a sacrifice' without naming the rule or testing peril has taken about half the marks available.

blocks.h: Why general average exists at all

blocks.p: It is far older than marine insurance and older than most maritime law - the principle is found in the Rhodian sea law and passed through Roman law into every modern maritime system. The problem it solves is one of incentives at the worst possible moment. If a master must jettison cargo to save the ship, and the loss lay entirely where it fell, then whoever owned that particular cargo would bear everything while the rest of the adventure was saved at his expense. Nobody would consent, and the master's decision would be contested at the moment when hesitation is most dangerous. Making the loss a shared loss removes the conflict: every interest knows that a sacrifice made for the common safety will be contributed to by all. Seen that way, general average is a rule about decision-making under peril, not really a rule about money.

blocks.h: Sacrifice versus accident - the line that decides everything

blocks.p: Almost every general average problem in an examination is a disguised question about whether the loss was chosen. Cargo swept overboard by a sea is an accident; cargo jettisoned is a sacrifice. An engine that fails on passage is an accident; an engine deliberately worked to destruction to refloat the ship is a sacrifice. Water damage from a leak is an accident; water damage from firefighting is a sacrifice. Rule VII is simply that same line drawn for one specific case - and the drafters drew it so firmly that they added an absolute prohibition for the afloat case, because otherwise every hard manoeuvre would generate a claim.

blocks.h: The four conditions of Rule VII, and which one is really in issue

blocks.p: Ashore; in a position of peril; an actual intention to float her for the common safety; at the risk of such damage. In practice the first and third are usually obvious on the facts and the fourth follows from them. The condition that is actually litigated is peril. A ship aground is not automatically in peril - the question is whether she was in real danger, having regard to the bottom, the weather, the tide, her condition and the exposure of the position. That is why a careful answer says the claim 'turns on establishing peril' rather than simply asserting it, and why the master's log, weather records and any surveyor's evidence matter so much afterwards.

blocks.h: Which version of the Rules applies

blocks.p: The York-Antwerp Rules are contractual, not statutory. They apply because the bill of lading or charterparty says they do, which is why the Rule of Interpretation has to declare that they operate 'to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith'. The consequence is that the version in force between the parties may be the 1994, 2004 or 2016 text, depending on what the contract incorporates. On this question it does not matter: Rule VII is materially identical in all three. On other questions it can matter a great deal, so the habit of asking which version is incorporated is worth forming.

quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) 'yes, it is a general average sacrifice' without naming Rule VII, without testing whether the ship was in a position of peril, and without stating the converse. Rule VII allows the claim only where the ship is ashore and in peril and the machinery was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety at the risk of such damage - and it then prohibits absolutely, 'in any circumstances', any allowance for machinery damage caused by working the propelling machinery while the ship is afloat. The same burnt bearings are therefore general average or particular average according to the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked. A second trap in limb (a) is forgetting that there must be a common adventure: a ship in ballast with no cargo has no general average, because there is no other interest to contribute.

questions.understand_first: General average is not insurance and not liability - it is a rule of contribution, and it is one of the oldest ideas in maritime law. The problem it solves is a problem of incentives at the worst moment: if the master must sacrifice one interest to save the whole adventure, and the loss lay entirely where it fell, the owner of that interest would be ruined for everyone else's benefit and would fight the decision. Making the loss shared removes the conflict. Everything in limb (a) follows from that purpose - the sacrifice must be deliberate (or there was no decision to protect), for the common safety (or there is nothing to share), and reasonable (or the decision does not deserve protection). And limb (b) is simply that same test applied to an engine: damage suffered because the master chose to risk the machinery to save the ship is a sacrifice; damage suffered in the ordinary course is not.

Limb (b) is Rule VII as four conditions and one prohibition (5-6): ashore, in peril, intending to refloat, accepting the risk - but never afloat.
