retrieval_cards.prompt: State the Rule A definition of a general average act.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: The essential features are the clauses of this sentence. Quote it and the features write themselves.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the essential difference between general average and particular average?
retrieval_cards.answer: General average loss is intentionally and reasonably incurred for the common safety of the whole adventure, and is shared rateably by all the contributing interests. Particular average is accidental damage which falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared. The dividing line is whether the loss was chosen.
retrieval_cards.why: Almost every general average problem is a disguised question about whether the loss was deliberate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Quote Rule VII of the York-Antwerp Rules.
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.
retrieval_cards.why: It decides limb (b) outright. The second half - the absolute prohibition when afloat - is the part candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A grounded vessel's main engine bearings burn out while working ahead and astern to refloat her. Is the damage general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, under Rule VII, provided four things are shown: that she was ashore; that she was in a position of peril; that the machinery was worked with an actual intention to float her for the common safety; and that the damage arose at the risk of such damage. Working ahead and astern to shake her loose establishes the intention and the acceptance of risk. Peril is the condition that must actually be proved.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner asks for justification, so the marks are in applying the four conditions rather than in the yes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Would the answer change if the ship had already been afloat when the bearings burnt?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, completely. Rule VII provides that where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average. The identical damage would be particular average - the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy and not shared with cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: Same physical damage, opposite legal answer. What decides it is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The grounding was caused by the master's negligence. Does that defeat the general average claim?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Rule D provides that rights to contribution in general average shall not be affected though the event which gave rise to the sacrifice may have been due to the fault of one of the parties to the common maritime adventure, but without prejudice to any remedies or defences open against or to that party in respect of that fault. The adjustment proceeds; blame is dealt with separately.
retrieval_cards.why: It keeps the adjustment moving. Cargo interests can still sue the owner for the fault - they simply cannot use it to refuse to contribute.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship is in ballast with no cargo on board and you sacrifice equipment to save her. Is there general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Rule A requires the act to be for the common safety and for the purpose of preserving property involved in a common maritime adventure. With no cargo there is only one interest at risk, no common adventure and nothing to contribute, so the loss falls entirely on the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: The word common in the definition is a condition, not decoration, and this is the quickest way to test whether it has been understood.

blocks.h: 1. (a) The mandatory basis in SOLAS and MARPOL

ul: SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 is the operative provision. Adopted by resolution MSC.257(84), it makes Parts I and II of the Casualty Investigation Code mandatory and took effect on 1 January 2010 - converting investigation from an undertaking into an obligation.

SOLAS regulation I/21 is the older and broader provision: each Administration undertakes to conduct an investigation of any casualty occurring to its ships subject to the Convention when it judges that the investigation may assist in identifying what changes to the Convention might be desirable.

MARPOL Article 12 - Casualties to ships: each Administration undertakes to investigate any casualty occurring to its ships subject to the Convention where the casualty has produced a major deleterious effect upon the marine environment, and to supply the Organization with information concerning the findings.

Behind both sits UNCLOS Article 94(7), requiring an inquiry into marine casualties on the high seas involving loss of life, serious injury to another State's nationals, or serious damage to ships, installations or the environment. The Code cites SOLAS I/21 and UNCLOS 94(7) together.

blocks.h: 2. (b) The purpose and structure of the Code

blocks.p: The Code - resolution MSC.255(84) - provides a common approach to marine safety investigations. Its defining principle, and the thing to state first, is that a marine safety investigation is conducted to prevent future casualties, not to apportion blame or determine liability. It is separate from, and must not be prejudiced by, any criminal, disciplinary or civil proceedings. It is arranged in three parts:

ul: Part I - General provisions (chapters 1 to 3): purpose, definitions and application.
Part II - Mandatory standards (from chapter 4): what a State Party must do.
Part III - Recommended practices (from chapter 15): what it should do.
An impartial Marine Safety Investigation Authority (chapter 4), properly resourced.

Notification (chapter 5) - ship name and flag, IMO number, nature, location, time and date, numbers seriously injured or killed, consequences to persons, property and environment, and any other ship involved.
A safety investigation into every very serious marine casualty (chapter 6.1), with the flag State responsible for ensuring it is conducted and completed (6.2).

Agreement between substantially interested States (chapter 7) - the flag State may agree that another State conducts the investigation, and participating in it discharges its obligations under the Code, SOLAS I/21 and UNCLOS 94(7).
Powers of investigation, parallel investigations and co-operation (chapters 8 to 10).
Independence (chapter 11) - the investigation shall not be subject to external direction.
Obtaining evidence from seafarers (chapter 12) - they are informed of the nature and basis of the investigation and may be legally represented.
Draft reports (chapter 13) circulated to substantially interested States for comment, normally within 30 days.

Reports (chapter 14) - the final report of every very serious marine casualty investigation is submitted to the Organization, and so is any other report containing information that may prevent future casualties.
Administrative responsibilities and principles of investigation (chapters 15 and 16), and guidance on investigating casualties and incidents.
Confidentiality of marine safety records - statements, communications, medical and private information, analyses and voyage data recorder information - so that people speak freely to investigators.
Protection for witnesses and involved parties, notification to parties involved, co-ordination, evidence collection, and the re-opening of an investigation where significant new evidence emerges.

blocks.p: The Code defines it at paragraph 2.22: "A very serious marine casualty means a marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship or a death or severe damage to the environment." Three limbs, any one of which is sufficient. Reading it needs the supporting definitions: a marine casualty (2.9) is an event, or sequence of events, resulting directly in connection with the operation of a ship in death or serious injury, loss of a person overboard, loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship, or material damage; a serious injury (2.18) is one causing incapacitation for more than 72 hours commencing within seven days of the injury; and severe damage to the environment (2.19) is damage which, as evaluated by the affected State or the flag State, produces a major deleterious effect upon the environment.

The classification matters because it triggers obligations: a safety investigation is mandatory for every very serious marine casualty, and the final report must go to IMO. Note also that the Code defines only this term - the related expression "serious marine casualty" appears nowhere in it and comes from IMO's separate reporting guidance.

Three printed limbs and a clear weighting: (a) is a citation question, (b) is the bulk, and (c) is a definition. Give roughly 4, 8 and 4. Limb (a) is answered in a few lines if you know the regulation numbers and lost entirely if you do not, so learn them; limb (c) is worth quoting almost verbatim. Do not let limb (b) sprawl - the word is briefly, and a structured list of the Code's mandatory standards scores better than prose.

blocks.h: The one sentence that must appear

blocks.p: A marine safety investigation is conducted to prevent future casualties, not to apportion blame or determine liability. That is the Code's whole philosophy, and everything else follows from it - why investigations must be independent of external direction, why marine safety records are confidential, why witnesses are protected, and why the investigation is kept separate from criminal and civil proceedings. If an answer omits it, the examiner cannot tell whether the candidate understands the Code or has merely listed its chapters.

Three provisions, and they do different jobs. SOLAS XI-1/6 is the mandatory hook - it makes Parts I and II of the Code mandatory and took effect on 1 January 2010. SOLAS I/21 is the older, discretionary undertaking, where the Administration investigates when it judges the investigation may assist in identifying desirable changes to the Convention. MARPOL Article 12 is the pollution counterpart, and note its threshold - a major deleterious effect upon the marine environment. Citing only XI-1/6 answers half of limb (a), because the question expressly asks for SOLAS and MARPOL.

ul: Giving only the SOLAS provision when the question asks for SOLAS and MARPOL. MARPOL Article 12 is the one - an Article, not a regulation in an Annex.
Confusing "very serious marine casualty" with "serious marine casualty". Only the first is defined in the Code; the second comes from IMO's reporting guidance and is not in MSC.255(84) at all.
Writing that the purpose of an investigation is to find who was at fault. It is the opposite, and it is the single most important point in the question.
Getting the serious-injury definition loosely. It is incapacitation for more than 72 hours, commencing within seven days of the injury.
Treating the whole Code as mandatory. Parts I and II are mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/6; Part III is recommended practice, and the question asks about both.
Forgetting that the final report of every very serious marine casualty investigation goes to IMO.

blocks.p:
"A crew member died - is that a very serious marine casualty?" Yes. The three limbs are total loss of the ship, or a death, or severe damage to the environment - any one is sufficient, and a death alone qualifies.

"Who investigates if the ship is Indian-flagged but the casualty is in another State's waters?" The flag State is responsible, but chapter 7 allows agreement with another substantially interested State to conduct it, and participation in that investigation discharges the flag State's obligations under the Code, SOLAS I/21 and UNCLOS 94(7).

"Can the investigation report be used in court?" The Code makes safety records confidential and keeps the safety investigation separate from criminal, disciplinary and civil proceedings, precisely so that evidence is given freely. That separation is a design feature, not an oversight.

ul: Which regulation makes the Casualty Investigation Code mandatory, and from when? SOLAS regulation XI-1/6, adopted by MSC.257(84), effective 1 January 2010.
Define a very serious marine casualty. A marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship, or a death, or severe damage to the environment.

What is a substantially interested State? Broadly: the flag State, the coastal State, a State whose environment was severely or significantly damaged, one whose nationals died or were seriously injured, or one with a significant interest recognised by the investigating State.

What is the difference between a marine casualty and a marine incident? An incident endangers, or would endanger if not corrected, the ship, its occupants or the environment - but it stops short of the outcomes that make a casualty, and it excludes deliberate acts intended to cause harm.
What must the notification contain? Ship name and flag, IMO number, nature, location, time and date, numbers seriously injured or killed, consequences, and any other ship involved.
Where does the final report go? To the Organization, for every very serious marine casualty investigation.

blocks.p: WHY - WHO - WHAT - WHEN. Why: prevention, not blame. Who: an independent Marine Safety Investigation Authority, with the flag State responsible and substantially interested States able to take over. What: notify, investigate, take evidence, draft, circulate for 30 days, report to IMO. When: mandatory for every very serious marine casualty. For the definition itself: SHIP - LIFE - SEA - total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment.

One point is worth stating carefully. The Code defines only "very serious marine casualty"; a search of the full Code text returns no occurrence of the expression "serious marine casualty" standing alone. That term belongs to IMO's separate casualty-reporting guidance, which sits outside the Code and has been revised over time. This answer therefore gives the Code's definition and identifies the other term as coming from elsewhere, rather than presenting a graded scale as though the Code contained one. The Code has also been amended since its 2008 adoption; the material relied on here - purpose, structure, the chapter 6 investigation duty and the chapter 2 definitions - is the stable core, but a candidate citing a specific paragraph number in an oral should be ready to say which edition they are quoting.

questions.understand_first: A marine safety investigation is not a trial, and the Code exists to keep it from becoming one. retrieval_cards.answer: Code paragraph 2.22 - a marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship or a death or severe damage to the environment. Any one of the three limbs is sufficient.
retrieval_cards.why: Worth quoting verbatim; it is a four-mark definition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which SOLAS regulation makes the Code mandatory, and from when?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS regulation XI-1/6, adopted by resolution MSC.257(84), making Parts I and II of the Code mandatory with effect from 1 January 2010.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which MARPOL provision requires casualty investigation?
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Article 12 - Casualties to ships. The Administration investigates any casualty to its ships where it has produced a major deleterious effect upon the marine environment, and supplies the findings to the Organization.
retrieval_cards.why: It is an Article of the Convention, not a regulation in an Annex - and the question asks for SOLAS AND MARPOL.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the purpose of a marine safety investigation?
retrieval_cards.answer: To prevent marine casualties and incidents in the future. It is not to apportion blame or determine liability, and it is kept separate from criminal, disciplinary and civil proceedings.
retrieval_cards.why: The Code's founding principle - omit it and the answer looks like a chapter list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is "serious marine casualty" defined in the Casualty Investigation Code?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Code defines only "very serious marine casualty", at 2.22. The other expression comes from IMO's separate casualty-reporting guidance and does not appear in the Code.
retrieval_cards.why: A confidently made error - candidates often present a graded scale the Code does not contain.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is "serious injury" defined?
retrieval_cards.answer: An injury resulting in incapacitation where the person is unable to function normally for more than 72 hours, commencing within seven days from the date the injury was suffered.
retrieval_cards.why: Both numbers are examinable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which parts of the Code are mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: Parts I and II, through SOLAS XI-1/6. Part I is general provisions and definitions, Part II the mandatory standards from chapter 4. Part III contains recommended practices from chapter 15.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to the final investigation report?
retrieval_cards.answer: For every very serious marine casualty, the final report is submitted to the Organization. Other reports are also submitted where they contain information that may prevent or lessen the seriousness of future casualties.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish a marine casualty from a marine incident.
retrieval_cards.answer: A casualty has resulted in death or serious injury, loss of a person overboard, loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship, or material damage. An incident endangered, or would have endangered if uncorrected, the ship, its occupants or the environment - and excludes deliberate acts intended to cause harm.

blocks.h: 1. A) What the human element means in STCW

blocks.p: STCW refuses to treat competence as something that time served automatically confers. It replaces experience with demonstrated competence, and then addresses the conditions - fitness, rest, teamwork and company responsibility - under which competence can actually be exercised. The instrument is the STCW Convention and Code, 1978, as amended, most significantly by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force from 1 January 2012.

ul: The Part A tables of competence specify, for every function and level, the competence required, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency behind it, the methods for demonstrating it and the criteria for evaluating it - so assessment is against a published standard, not an examiner's impression.
Part A is mandatory; Part B is guidance - a distinction worth stating explicitly.

The Manila amendments added mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level - where engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management enter the Convention. It is the explicit recognition that technically competent individuals still fail as a team.
Regulation I/6 governs training and assessment, and regulation I/8 requires a quality standards system, so the training system itself is audited rather than assumed.
Regulation I/11 requires periodic revalidation, and chapter VI mandatory safety familiarisation and basic training before a seafarer is assigned duties.

blocks.h: 3. Fitness for duty - the physical human being

ul: Regulation VIII/1 requires each Administration, for the purpose of preventing fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods for watchkeeping personnel and for those with designated safety, security and pollution-prevention duties in accordance with section A-VIII/1, and to require that watch systems are arranged so that efficiency is not impaired by fatigue.

The Manila-amended A-VIII/1 minimum rest is 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.

Authorised exceptions are tightly conditioned: weekly rest may not fall below 70 hours in any 7-day period, exceptions from the 77-hour norm may not run for more than two consecutive weeks, and daily rest may then be divided into no more than three periods.
The Manila amendments also introduced alcohol limits for masters, officers and other seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.
Regulation I/9 sets medical fitness standards, and regulation VIII/2 with section A-VIII/2 governs watchkeeping arrangements and principles.

blocks.h: 4. Responsibility placed on companies and Administrations

blocks.p: Regulation I/14 makes the company responsible for ensuring that seafarers hold valid certificates, are familiarised with their duties and with the ship's arrangements, and that documentation is maintained - so the human element is not left as an individual's problem. Administrations operate quality standards systems and are subject to independent evaluation and reporting to IMO.

blocks.h: 5. B) The IMO guidance on fatigue

blocks.p: The guidance is MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', of 24 January 2019, approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee and finalized by the HTW Sub-Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory - the binding rest-hour requirements remain in STCW chapter VIII and in MLC 2006. The Guidelines are arranged in six modules, each addressed to a different party:

ul: Module 1 - Fatigue: what it is and its causes, grouped as sleep and rest, the biological clock and circadian rhythm, health and stress, environmental factors such as noise, vibration and motion, sleep disorders and operational factors. It defines sleep debt as insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods.
Module 2 - Fatigue and the Company: assessing, mitigating and managing fatigue risk in the safety management system, in manning decisions and in scheduling.

Module 3 - Fatigue and the Seafarer: practical guidance for the master, officers and ratings on sleep quality, diet and the limits of countermeasures - notably that caffeine is not a substitute for sleep.
Module 4 - Fatigue Awareness and Training.
Module 5 - Fatigue and Ship Design: mitigation designed in - accommodation location, noise, vibration, lighting and habitability.
Module 6 - Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities: how regulators and inspectors should approach it.

blocks.h: 6. How the guidance and the rules fit together

blocks.p: The Guidelines are explicit that hours of rest are set by a prescriptive formula in STCW chapter VIII, and that complying with the formula is not the same as being rested: managers must allow for circadian rhythm and sleep debt, and - in the Guidelines' own words - rest means rest, not the substitution of a different form of work. The same theme runs through MLC 2006 Regulations 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7. A management-level engineer should therefore treat recorded compliance as the floor, and a rest-hour record that is always exactly compliant as a warning rather than a reassurance.

Two printed limbs of 8 marks each, so split the answer evenly and head each limb clearly. Limb A rewards structure - competence tables, fitness for duty, company responsibility - and limb B rewards naming the actual circular. A candidate who writes generally about tiredness for the second limb without producing MSC.1/Circ.1598 and its module structure will lose most of eight marks, because 'the IMO guidance' is a specific document.

blocks.h: The organising idea for limb A

blocks.p: STCW attacks the human element on three fronts, and saying so gives the limb a spine: can they do it (competence standards, assessed against published criteria), are they fit to do it now (fitness for duty - rest, medical, alcohol), and who is responsible for making that possible (regulation I/14, the company). The Manila amendments strengthened all three and added the fourth dimension the older Convention lacked - can they work as a team, through mandatory leadership and teamworking training.

blocks.h: The numbers you must get right

blocks.p: 10 hours in any 24, and 77 hours in any 7 days. Divided into no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rest periods. Exceptions may not go below 70 hours in any 7 days and may not run more than two consecutive weeks. Learn 10, 77, 2, 6, 14, 70 - and be careful, because 70 and 77 are both real figures doing different jobs: 77 is the norm, 70 is the floor under an authorised exception. Quoting 70 as the normal requirement is the classic error, and it is exactly the trap that a pre-2010 copy of the Code will lead you into.

This is worth a paragraph of its own because it caught this project. A freely available IMO circular copy of section A-VIII/1 - STCW.6/Circ.1 - reproduces the 1995 Code: five paragraphs, 70 hours weekly, and no 14-hour interval provision at all. It looks entirely authoritative, it is on an official domain, and it is superseded. A candidate who revises from it will write 70 where 77 is required and will omit the 14-hour rule altogether. The lesson generalises: for any instrument that has been amended, the question to ask of a source is not 'is this official?' but 'which edition is this?'

questions.understand_first: The phrase human element is not a polite word for human error. In STCW it means the whole set of conditions that decide whether a competent person actually performs competently on the day - whether the standard he was assessed against was published and objective, whether he has slept, whether he is medically fit, whether he can work as part of a team, and whether his company has made any of that possible. That is why limb A cannot be answered with rest hours alone: rest is one of four fronts. And it is why limb B is a separate document - the mandatory rule sets a floor for hours, while the Guidelines address the thing the floor cannot reach, which is whether the person is actually rested.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the minimum hours of rest under the Manila-amended section A-VIII/1.
retrieval_cards.answer: Not less than 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.
retrieval_cards.why: The 14-hour interval is the provision most often omitted, and its absence from a source is the quickest way to tell that the source is pre-Manila.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the weekly minimum rest 70 hours or 77 hours?
retrieval_cards.answer: 77 hours in any 7-day period is the norm. 70 hours is the floor that applies only where an exception has been authorised, and such an exception may not run for more than two consecutive weeks. Both figures are real; they do different jobs.
retrieval_cards.why: A widely available official IMO circular copy of A-VIII/1 is the pre-Manila 1995 text and gives 70 as the weekly figure. It is official and superseded - always check the edition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which circular is the IMO guidance on fatigue, and what did it replace?
retrieval_cards.answer: MSC.1/Circ.1598, Guidelines on fatigue, dated 24 January 2019 and approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 on Guidance on fatigue mitigation and management, approved at MSC 74 in 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb B says 'the IMO guidance' - a specific document. Naming it and its predecessor is most of the eight marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the six modules of MSC.1/Circ.1598.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Fatigue - what it is and its causes. 2 Fatigue and the Company. 3 Fatigue and the Seafarer. 4 Fatigue Awareness and Training. 5 Fatigue and Ship Design. 6 Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities.
retrieval_cards.why: Each module is addressed to a different party, which is the structural point: fatigue is managed by the company, the individual, the designer and the regulator, not only by the watchkeeper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the Manila amendments add to STCW on the human element?
retrieval_cards.answer: Mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and in leadership and managerial skill at management level - bringing engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management into the Convention; revised and tightened rest-hour requirements in section A-VIII/1 including the 14-hour interval rule; and alcohol limits for masters, officers and seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.
retrieval_cards.why: The teamworking addition is the recognition that technically competent individuals still fail as a crew, which is the analytical heart of limb A.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your engineer's rest-hour record is exactly compliant every single week. Is that reassuring?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - it is a warning. The Guidelines are explicit that hours of rest are a prescriptive formula and that complying with the formula is not the same as being rested; circadian rhythm and sleep debt determine whether rest is restorative. A record that is always exactly at the limit suggests the limit is driving the record rather than the work.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the management-level judgement the question is really testing, and it is what separates a Class I answer from a recitation of numbers.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does STCW regulation I/14 require of the company?
retrieval_cards.answer: That seafarers assigned to its ships hold valid certificates, are familiarised with their specific duties and with the ship's arrangements, installations, equipment and procedures before being assigned duties, and that documentation and data are maintained. It places the human element on the company rather than leaving it as an individual's problem.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb A is incomplete without the responsibility front, and I/14 is the provision that supplies it.

blocks.h: 1. What the Act means by an unseaworthy ship

blocks.p: The Merchant Shipping Act 1958 gives no definition of unseaworthiness in a definitions section. The description sits inside section 334 itself, which treats a ship as unseaworthy when the following are not such as to render her in every respect fit for the proposed voyage or service:

ul: the materials of which she is made and her construction;
the qualifications of the master;
the number, description and qualifications of the crew, including officers;
the weight, description and stowage of the cargo and ballast;
the condition of her hull and equipment, boilers and machinery.

blocks.p: Two features carry the marks. The test is relative - fitness for the proposed voyage or service - so a ship adequate for a sheltered coastal run may be unseaworthy for an ocean passage. And it is far wider than material condition: an undermanned ship, one whose officers hold the wrong certificates, or a mechanically perfect ship with badly stowed cargo is unseaworthy under the Act.

blocks.h: 2. The offence, and the defences the Act allows

ul: s.334(1) - every person who sends or attempts to send an Indian ship to sea from any port in India in such an unseaworthy state that the life of any person is likely to be thereby endangered is guilty of an offence, unless he proves he used all reasonable means to insure her being sent to sea in a seaworthy state, or that sending her to sea in that state was, in the circumstances, reasonable and justifiable.
s.334(2) - a master who knowingly takes such a ship to sea commits the offence, with only the second defence available to him.
s.334(3) permits a person charged to give evidence in his own defence; s.334(4) provides that no prosecution shall be instituted except by, or with the consent of, the Central Government.

blocks.p: Liability is therefore not automatic. The threshold is danger to life, the burden of the defence lies on the accused, and the standard demanded is reasonable means rather than a guarantee of result.

blocks.h: 3. What an unsafe ship is, and the power to detain her

blocks.p: Section 336 is directed at a different problem - stopping the ship rather than punishing anybody. An unsafe ship is one which, by reason of the defective condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of overloading or improper loading, is unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of the service for which she is intended. The procedure is staged:

ol: the Central Government, having reason to believe on complaint or otherwise that she is unsafe, may order her provisionally detained for the purpose of survey;
a written statement of the grounds must be served forthwith on the master;
the matter is referred to the court of survey for the port, or a competent person is appointed to survey the ship and report;
on that report she is either released or finally detained.

blocks.h: 4. The real difference between the two

ul: Unseaworthy is a state; unsafe is the trigger for a power. Section 334 describes a condition and attaches criminal liability to sending a ship to sea in it. Section 336 describes a condition that entitles the Government to stop her.
One looks backwards, the other forwards. The offence punishes a decision already taken; detention prevents the voyage from happening at all.
Unseaworthiness is the wider concept - it expressly takes in crew numbers and qualifications and the stowage of cargo and ballast. The unsafe-ship definition lists a narrower set of causes.
The thresholds differ - life likely to be endangered under s.334; unfitness to proceed without serious danger to human life under s.336.
In practice, a ship unsafe within s.336 will invariably be unseaworthy within s.334, but a ship may be unseaworthy - one certificated engineer short - without being unsafe.

blocks.h: 5. The owner's obligation to the crew

blocks.p: Section 335 converts seaworthiness from a matter between owner and cargo into a duty owed to the people on board. In every contract of service, express or implied, between the owner of an Indian ship and the master or any seaman, and in every contract of apprenticeship, there is implied - notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary - an obligation that the owner, the master and every agent charged with the loading of the ship, or preparing her for sea, or sending her to sea shall use all reasonable means to ensure the seaworthiness of the ship for the voyage at the time when the voyage commences, and shall keep her in a seaworthy state during the voyage.

Three consequences follow. The duty is non-excludable - a term in the crew agreement waiving it is void. It is a due diligence standard, not a warranty of result. And it is continuing throughout the voyage rather than being discharged at departure. It also binds people other than the registered owner: the loading agent is named in the section.

blocks.h: 6. How the obligation is policed, and the statute in force at this sitting

blocks.p: Section 335(2) allows the Central Government, on the owner's request or otherwise, to arrange a survey of the hull, equipment or machinery. In practice the duty is policed through the wider system - class and flag State statutory survey and certification, ISM auditing, and port State control under SOLAS chapter I regulation 19 - with the section 336 detention power as the last resort.

One point of currency should be stated rather than assumed. The Merchant Shipping Act 1958 was the operative law on the examination date, and there was at this sitting no other candidate for that role. The Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024 - the Bill that became the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 - had been introduced in the Lok Sabha on 10 December 2024 and was still before Parliament: it was passed by the Lok Sabha only on 6 August 2025 and by the Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2025, received assent on 18 August 2025 as Act No. 24 of 2025, and was brought into force only on 15 March 2026, when section 324(1) repealed the 1958 Act. A Bill is not an Act, and assent is not commencement. Every one of those steps came after this paper was sat, so the answer is correctly and necessarily given on the 1958 Act.

The comparison in step 4 is the highest-value paragraph in the answer and the one most often missing: candidates define both terms and then never say how they differ, which is literally what was asked.

blocks.h: Why the Act splits the idea in two

blocks.p: A criminal offence needs fault, a trial and proof beyond reasonable doubt, and it operates after the event - which is no use at all to the crew of a ship that is about to sail. An administrative detention power needs only a reasonable belief and can act within hours. The 1958 Act therefore does both: section 334 attaches consequences to a decision, and section 336 supplies the fast preventive lever, with the survey and the right to be told the grounds as the safeguards against its misuse. Seeing that the two sections exist to solve different problems is the whole of the distinction.

blocks.h: Seaworthiness has three different legal lives - keep them apart

ul: Statutory and criminal - MSA 1958 s.334, which is this question. A state of the ship, punishable, with a due-diligence defence.
Contractual, owed to the crew - MSA 1958 s.335. Implied, non-excludable, and continuing through the voyage.

Insurance and carriage - a warranty or a duty of due diligence depending on whether the policy is a voyage or a time policy and on the contract of carriage. Under Indian law that is the Marine Insurance Act 1963, not the English Act of 1906, and a breach affects recovery rather than attracting a penalty.

blocks.p: The examiner asks about the first two. Answering about the third is the commonest way to lose this question.

blocks.h: A Bill is not an Act - and this sitting proves it

blocks.p: A candidate sitting this paper in June 2025 could easily have read about the new Merchant Shipping Bill and assumed the 1958 Act was on its way out. It was, but it had not gone. The Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 10 December 2024 and, at this examination, had been passed by neither House. It cleared the Lok Sabha on 6 August 2025, the Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2025, received the assent of the President on 18 August 2025, and even then did not become law: an Indian Act ordinarily commences on a date the Central Government appoints by notification in the Official Gazette, and here that notification, S.O. 1244(E), appointed 15 March 2026. So the ladder has four rungs - introduced, passed, assented, commenced - and in June 2025 the Bill was still on the first. That is the same staged problem Q2 of this paper examines for an international convention, where adoption, ratification and entry into force are three different things, and the two are worth revising together.

Prosecution requires Central Government consent. Unsafe - s.336. A ship which by reason of defective hull, equipment or machinery, or overloading or improper loading, is unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of her intended service. She may be provisionally detained for survey, with written grounds served forthwith on the master, then finally detained or released after report by a court of survey or an appointed surveyor. Difference. Unseaworthy is a state attracting criminal liability and a duty; unsafe is the trigger for a preventive power. Unseaworthiness is wider and takes in crew and stowage; unsafe lists its causes and demands serious danger to life. Every unsafe ship is unseaworthy; not every unseaworthy ship is unsafe. Owner to crew - s.335. An obligation implied into every contract of service and of apprenticeship, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, that the owner, the master and every agent charged with loading, preparing or sending her to sea shall use all reasonable means to ensure seaworthiness at the commencement of the voyage and to keep her in a seaworthy state during the voyage. The Central Government may arrange a survey under s.335(2). Statute on the day. The 1958 Act governed, and nothing else was in the running: its replacement was still the Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024, introduced 10 December 2024 and passed by neither House. It was passed in August 2025, assented 18 August 2025 and commenced only 15 March 2026.

questions.understand_first: These are two different legal tools, not two words for the same idea. Unseaworthy describes a state of the ship and is the trigger for a criminal offence and for a duty owed to the crew - it asks who is to blame. Unsafe is the trigger for an administrative power: it lets the Government stop the ship before anyone is hurt - it asks whether this ship sails today. Note also that seaworthiness here is far wider than hull and machinery: an undermanned or badly stowed ship is unseaworthy under the Act even if she is mechanically perfect.
questions.memory_cue: STATE (1-2) - POWER (3) - COMPARE (4) - DUTY (5) - POLICE (6). The section trio is consecutive and in that order: 334 unseaworthy, 335 the owner's duty, 336 unsafe and detention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes a ship unseaworthy under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958?
retrieval_cards.answer: Her materials, construction, the master's qualifications, the number, description and qualifications of the crew including officers, the weight, description and stowage of cargo and ballast, and the condition of hull, equipment, boilers and machinery being not such as to render her in every respect fit for the proposed voyage or service.
retrieval_cards.why: Section 334. Crew and stowage are inside the definition - unseaworthiness is not only a material condition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is an unsafe ship under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958?
retrieval_cards.answer: A ship which, by reason of the defective condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of overloading or improper loading, is unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of the service for which she is intended.
retrieval_cards.why: Section 336. The listed causes and the serious-danger threshold are what make it narrower than unseaworthiness.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the essential difference between an unseaworthy ship and an unsafe ship.
retrieval_cards.answer: Unseaworthy describes a state of the ship and founds a criminal offence and a duty owed to the crew; unsafe is the trigger for an administrative power to detain her before she sails. Unseaworthiness is the wider concept. Every unsafe ship is unseaworthy, but not every unseaworthy ship is unsafe.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the analytical mark in the question, and it is the sentence most candidates never write.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What obligation does section 335 imply, and can it be contracted out of?
retrieval_cards.answer: An obligation implied into every contract of service and of apprenticeship that the owner, the master and every agent charged with loading, preparing or sending the ship to sea shall use all reasonable means to ensure seaworthiness at the commencement of the voyage and keep her seaworthy during it. It applies notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, so it cannot be contracted out of.
retrieval_cards.why: The non-excludable character is the point of the section, and that phrase is the one to quote.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the owner's obligation under section 335 an absolute guarantee of seaworthiness?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The obligation is to use all reasonable means to ensure seaworthiness at the commencement of the voyage and to keep her in a seaworthy state during it. It is a due-diligence standard, not a warranty of result.
retrieval_cards.why: The words all reasonable means are doing the work, and section 334 offers the same standard as a defence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Set out the procedure for detaining an unsafe ship under section 336.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Central Government, having reason to believe on complaint or otherwise that the ship is unsafe, may order her provisionally detained for survey. A written statement of the grounds must be served forthwith on the master. The matter is referred to the court of survey for the port, or a competent person is appointed to survey and report. On that report she is either released or finally detained.
retrieval_cards.why: Four stages, and the written grounds served on the master is the safeguard candidates most often omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Merchant Shipping Act governed this June 2025 examination, and why is that not obvious?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act 1958. The Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024, which became the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, had been introduced in the Lok Sabha on 10 December 2024 but had been passed by neither House at this sitting. It was passed on 6 and 11 August 2025, assented on 18 August 2025, and commenced only on 15 March 2026. Until then the 1958 Act applied in full.
retrieval_cards.why: A Bill is not an Act, and assent is not commencement. Reform that is being reported in the press is not yet law.
